candidate.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — newborn hearing screening
candidate.educational_objective: Explain the universal newborn hearing-screening benchmark and the importance of timely follow-up when a newborn does not pass screening.

options.A: Only newborns with a documented family history of childhood hearing loss need screening.
options.B: All newborns should complete hearing screening by 1 month of age so possible hearing loss can be identified and followed promptly.
options.C: Hearing screening should wait until speech delay becomes apparent in early childhood.
options.D: Routine screening is unnecessary because congenital hearing loss cannot be detected in the newborn period.

candidate.rationale: CDC Early Hearing Detection and Intervention guidance uses the 1-3-6 benchmarks: hearing screening by 1 month of age, diagnostic evaluation by 3 months for infants who do not pass, and enrollment in early intervention by 6 months when hearing loss is diagnosed. CDC specifically directs health professionals to ensure the hearing-screening process is complete for all newborns. B is correct.
candidate.source_claim_supported: CDC directs health professionals to ensure the hearing-screening process is complete for all newborns by 1 month, with diagnostic evaluation by 3 months for infants who do not pass and timely intervention thereafter.
candidate.source_document_title: Information About Hearing Loss in Children for Health Professionals
